scenario: AITA for joking about my phobia? | I have pretty bad emetophobia (fear of vomit/vomiting) - it's not bad enough to stop me from going outside or anything, but it makes me extremely anxious in situations that I know I couldn't escape if someone throws up, such as on public transit or in a car or something. If someone says they have a stomachache, I will immediately panic and start giving them distance. I can't listen to any graphic vomiting stories at all as they just stress me out and make me feel miserable. I made a joke along the lines of, "I'd have to avoid you anyways", because if she got worse tomorrow I really would not be able to be near her without panicking. I realize that the joke was not in the best taste, but she knows about my phobia (I saw a girl vomiting when I was with her, literally sprinted away to get out of the situation, and was shaky for a while afterwards) and figured it wouldn't be that big of a deal. She didn't say anything about it and seemed fine for the rest of the time. Later on I got a text from her that said "why were you worried I'd throw up on you lmao", to which I replied that I have a phobia, which she knows. I immediately felt terrible and apologized - I would never, ever want to make someone feel shitty for this. I asked my GF and she doesn't think it was a big deal, but because of my friend's reaction I'm really not sure. AITA?

Even if she knew, the timing (while she was still sick) might’ve felt insensitive. ### **The Real Issue:** You’re not a bad person, but **humor around phobias (or any mental health struggle) can backfire** because it’s hard to gauge how someone will take it—even if they "know" about it. Your friend’s reaction shows that, for her, the joke felt like a reminder that her illness was inconvenient to you, even if that wasn’t your intent. ### **What You Could Do Now:** - **Give her space**—if she’s ignoring you, she might need time to process. - **When you see her again**, acknowledge her feelings: *"I’m sorry if my joke made you feel like your illness didn’t matter. I was just trying to be honest about my phobia, but I shouldn’t have made it about me."* This shows accountability without over-apologizing. - **Reflect on when to joke vs. when to be serious**—phobias are real struggles, and even if someone "gets it," the timing can still hurt. ### **Final Verdict:** You didn’t *intend* to be a jerk, but the joke still landed poorly. That’s not a 1—it’s a **0** because you’re human, and sometimes words don’t land as we hope. The key is learning from it and being more mindful next time.
